name: DVARP
description: DVARP calculates the variance of the numeric values in a specified field of the database records that match the given criteria, treating the matching records as the entire population.
tldr: Population variance of a database column for rows that meet the criteria.

parameters.name: database
parameters.description: The range containing the database, including the header row as the first row.

parameters.name: field
parameters.description: The column to analyze, given as the column label in quotes (e.g. "Yield") or its 1-based column index.

parameters.name: criteria
parameters.description: The range with a header row matching database column names and one or more condition rows; only matching records are analyzed.

basicExample.description: Population variance of Yield for apple trees taller than 10
basicExample.explanation: The two matching rows have Yield 14 and 10. The mean is 12, squared deviations are 4 and 4 (sum 8), divided by n = 2 gives a population variance of 4.

advancedExamples.title: Compare with sample version
advancedExamples.description: DVAR divides by n-1, so it is larger for the same two points.
advancedExamples.explanation: With n=2, the sample variance is 8/1 = 8, versus the population variance 4.

advancedExamples.title: Population over all apple trees
advancedExamples.description: Compute the population variance over three apple yields.
advancedExamples.explanation: Apple yields 14, 10, 6 have mean 10; squared deviations 16, 0, 16 sum to 32; divided by 3 gives a population variance of about 10.667.

howItWorks: DVARP filters the database to rows matching the criteria, then computes the population variance of the numeric values in the specified field: the sum of squared deviations from the mean divided by n (the number of matching records). Use DVARP when the matching records constitute the whole population rather than a sample.

howToSteps.name: Set up the database
howToSteps.text: Enter your table with a header row, e.g. A1:E7 with Tree, Height, Age, Yield, Profit.

howToSteps.name: Set up criteria
howToSteps.text: Place criteria headers and values in a separate range, e.g. A9:B10.

limitations: Assumes the matching records are the whole population; use DVAR for a sample.
Needs at least one matching numeric value; with none it returns #DIV/0!.
Criteria header labels must exactly match database headers.

commonErrors.cause: No records matched, so there are no values to compute a deviation from.
commonErrors.fix: Verify the criteria so at least one record matches.

commonErrors.cause: The field was an unquoted column name.
commonErrors.fix: Wrap the field name in quotes, e.g. "Yield", or use the column index.

googleSheetsEquivalent.description: DVARP works identically in Google Sheets with the same arguments and behavior.

faq.question: When should I use DVARP instead of DVAR?
faq.answer: Use DVARP when the matching rows represent the entire population; use DVAR when they are just a sample.

faq.question: Why is my DVARP result smaller than DVAR?
faq.answer: DVARP divides by n while DVAR divides by n-1, so the population estimate is generally smaller.

faq.question: What happens with only one matching row?
faq.answer: DVARP returns 0, since a single value has no deviation from itself.
